paper_title: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: This paper presents TurnTurk-GPT, a text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish obtained by fine-tuning a Turkish GPT-2 model with the TurnGPT objective on synthetic and real dialogue, and evaluates it on real Turkish conversation against rule baselines, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating the output of streaming speech recognisers, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. It outperforms the zero-shot language model only when the test speakers occur in training; on unseen speakers the two are statistically indistinguishable. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for a sentence-internal word, locating the Turkish end-of-turn cue in verb-final morphology. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when a speaker pauses the zero-shot and multilingual baselines remain close to chance. The model and the evaluation protocol are publicly released.

sections.content: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish Ahmet Tugrul Bayrak Data Science and Innovation Ata Technology Platforms Istanbul, Turkey tugrul.bayrak@atptech.com Fatma Nur Korkmaz Data Science and Innovation Ata Technology Platforms Istanbul, Turkey fatmanur.korkmaz@atptech.com Nur Yagmur Tuncer Data Science and Innovation Ata Technology Platforms Istanbul, Turkey yagmur.tuncer@atptech.com Mustafa Sertac Turkel Data Science and Innovation Ata Technology Platforms Istanbul, Turkey sertac.turkel@atptech.com AbstractThis paper presents TurnTurk-GPT, text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish obtained by fine-tuning Turkish GPT-2 model with the TurnGPT objective on synthetic and real dialogue, and evaluates it on real Turkish conversation against rule baselines, zero-shot Turkish language model and widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating the output of streaming speech recognisers, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. It outperforms the zero-shot language model only when the test speakers occur in training; on unseen speakers the two are statistically indistinguishable. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for sentence-internal word, locating the Turkish end-of-turn cue in verb-final morphology. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when speaker pauses the zero-shot and multilingual baselines remain close to chance. The model and the evaluation protocol are publicly released. Index Termsturn-taking, spoken dialogue systems, Turkish, language models, evaluation, synthetic data I. INTRODUCTION Conversation proceeds through an orderly exchange of speaking turns, with gaps and overlaps measured in few hundred milliseconds [1]. spoken dialogue system that responds too early interrupts the user, whereas one that responds too late causes unnatural delays. The system therefore requires an incrementally updated estimate of whether the current position is plausible turn ending [2], [3]. Text-based predictors treat this as token-level prediction problem inside language model [4]; audio-based predictors learn future voice activity from the waveform [5], [6]. Research models and benchmarks have focused on English, with multilingual work covering English, Mandarin and Japanese Accepted at ISAS 2026. 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. [7]; recent multi-domain benchmark is English-only [8]. Although deployed multilingual end-of-turn detectors list Turkish among their supported languages [9], their performance on real Turkish conversation has not been reported under public evaluation protocol. Turkish is verb-final and agglutinative, and its turn-final cues may differ substantially from those of English. Two Turkish resources for this task were introduced in previous work: Syn-TurnTurk, large corpus of dialogues generated by large language model [10], and Real-TurnTurk, small multimodal corpus of real dyadic conversations [11]. Real-TurnTurk was collected because openly available Turkish speech resources do not include spontaneous two-party conversation with speaker-separated audio and time-aligned transcripts: conversational corpora are either commercial or restricted to academic access on request, and open corpora consist of read or single-speaker recordings. Building on these two resources, TurnTurk-GPT, TurnGPT-style turn-taking predictor on Turkish backbone, is trained under four configurations combining synthetic and real data. It is evaluated under protocol defined for Turkish turn-taking prediction, which relies on word-level decision points, average precision, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. Within this protocol, TurnTurk-GPT is compared with zero-shot Turkish language model read in four ways and with multilingual end-of-turn detector used as released, and the conditions under which it improves on them are identified. Further analyses specific to Turkish show that the end-of-turn cue is carried by the suffixes of the final word, that the choice of tokeniser has substantial effect, that synthetic dialogue alone provides weak training signal, and that the text-only baselines remain close to chance level when the speaker pauses. In addition, the model is publicly available on Hugging Face as baseline for Turkish turn-taking prediction.1 1https://huggingface.co/tugrulbayrak/TurnTurk-Gpt II. RELATED WORK A. Turn-taking prediction Early systems determined turn ends with silence thresholds, which tend to interrupt speakers who pause and to respond late to speakers who finish quickly [3]. Continuous prediction replaced fixed thresholds: Roddy et al. [12] predict speech activity over future window and find acoustic and lexical features complementary. Voice Activity Projection [5] learns discretised future voice-activity patterns in self-supervised way; it has been run in real time [6] and extended to English, Mandarin and Japanese, where cross-lingual fine-tuning was found to transfer [7]. Evaluation remains fragmented across corpora and metrics, which recent benchmark efforts address for English [8]. B. Text-based models TurnGPT [4] adds turn-shift token to pre-trained transformer language model [13], [14] and trains it with the causal language modelling loss, so the turn-shift probability at each word depends only on preceding context and can be computed incrementally as words arrive. This formulation is adopted here. Production voice agents combine silence detection with text-based end-of-turn classifier that is queried on the recognisers transcript when the user stops speaking [9]; such classifier is evaluated here as baseline. Because pre-trained language model already assigns probabilities to sentence and document boundaries, it can also be read as zero-shot predictor without any turn-taking training; this is included as baseline that isolates what task-specific finetuning adds. C. Turkish Turkish is agglutinative and predominantly verb-final: tense, person, mood and question marking are expressed by suffixes on the clause-final verb, so the information that signals completion is concentrated at the end of the utterance and inside single word. Monolingual Turkish transformer language models have only recently become available [15]; one of them serves here as the backbone and as the zero-shot baseline. Publicly available turn-taking resources for Turkish consist of the two corpora introduced in previous work and used in this study [10], [11]. III. DATA Table summarises the corpora. Syn-TurnTurk2 contains topic-conditioned two-party dialogues generated by large language model [10]. Real-TurnTurk3 contains six dyadic video-call recordings with six distinct speakers, separate audio channels, per-channel voice activity detection, backchannel annotation and transcripts from the platforms live captioning [11]. Only the text and the turn structure are used. Real turns are derived from voice activity: consecutive segments of one speaker are merged into floor-holding turn, 2https://huggingface.co/datasets/tugrulbayrak/Syn-TurnTurk 3https://huggingface.co/datasets/tugrulbayrak/Real-TurnTurk TABLE DATA INFORMATION Dialogues / recordings Turns Words Mean words per turn Syn-TurnTurk Real-TurnTurk 6 578 15,531 26.9 1,625 14,185 123,397 8.7 0.02 0.61 0.74 <ts> bu is bitti <ts> evet anladım <ts> sp1 sp1 sp1 sp1 sp1 sp sp2 sp2 turn 1 (speaker A) turn 2 (speaker B) Fig. 1. Serialisation and scoring which backchannels do not split, and transcript segments are assigned to turns by temporal overlap. 4.7% of words lie in segments straddling turn boundary and 0.5% conflict with the voice activity annotation and are discarded [11]. Of 930 turn-internal pauses, 633 could be attributed to word, with median duration of 0.50 and 297 longer than 0.5 s; the remainder fall inside transcript segment and cannot be localised. These positions are the most likely points of interruption for deployed system and are used as hard negatives throughout. The difference in turn length between the corpora (Table I) indicates that they describe different phenomena: synthetic turns are short, complete sentences, whereas real turns are long, contain internal pauses, and are frequently resumed after backchannel. A. Model and objective IV. METHOD Following TurnGPT [4], turn-shift token <ts> and two speaker tokens are added to the vocabulary of turkish-gpt2 (124M parameters) [15]. dialogue is serialised as its turns, each closed by <ts>, with leading <ts>; speaker identity is supplied through token_type_ids. Training uses the causal language modelling loss, and the score of word is (<ts>) at its final subword token  (Fig. 1)  . B. Training configurations and input S: synthetic data only; R: real data only; SR: one stage on both; S2R: synthetic pre-training, then real fine-tuning. Optimisation uses fixed step budget, since the corpora differ in size by two orders of magnitude. Each configuration uses three seeds, averaged per position. The optimiser is AdamW with weight decay 0.01, linear schedule with 10% warm-up, gradient clipping at 1.0 and mixed precision. Training windows of 256 tokens overlap by half; at evaluation, every position is scored exactly once with at least 32 tokens of left context. Embeddings of the added tokens are initialised at the mean of the existing embeddings. The development set for early stopping is the final 12% of the windows of each training dialogue, with the adjacent window discarded to prevent overlap; validation loss is checked every 20 steps (50 for stages involving synthetic data) with patience of five checks. The synthetic stage holds out 5% of the dialogues for this purpose. The input is lower-cased text with punctuation removed, which approximates the output of streaming recognisers at decision time and corresponds to the normalisation used by the multilingual detector described below. The transcripts are final rather than streaming hypotheses, so all results are offline. A. Protocol V. EVALUATION laEvery word of the real corpus is decision point, belled positive if it ends its turn: 15,522 points, 578 positive. The primary metric is average precision (AP) [16]; random predictor scores 0.037. Precision, recall and F1 are taken at thresholds selected on the other folds (nested). Two splits are used: recording-disjoint (leave-one-recordingout), and speaker-disjoint, in which no speaker of the test recording appears in training (training shrinks to two or three recordings). Confidence intervals are recording-level cluster bootstrap intervals, and comparisons use paired cluster bootstrap on the same decision points [17]; difference is significant when the 95% interval excludes zero. Each of 2,000 bootstrap replicates draws six recordings with replacement and includes all decision points of every drawn recording; intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the replicate statistics. In paired comparisons both systems are evaluated on the same replicates. Because resampling is performed over recordings, the intervals reflect variation between conversations rather than between individual decision points. The false alarm rate is also reported on the 633 pre-pause negatives, words followed by turn-internal pause. B. Baselines B0 is random; B1 is turn-length prior estimated on the training folds. Zero-shot language model: The backbone without finetuning reads the same normalised words, with turns separated by newline. At each word, four readings are taken: (next {., ?, !}), (end of text), (newline) and their sum; the newline reading directly estimates the probability that the line, and therefore the turn, ends. Multilingual detector: The LiveKit multilingual turn detector [9] is used as released, through the inference code of its own framework, with its own normalisation (lower-casing, punctuation removal) and context. Its input contains the current turn up to the word being scored. VI. At its recommended Turkish threshold (0.0045), the detector predicts turn end at most positions: recall 0.881, precision 0.045, and 85.5% false alarms on pre-pause words. Second, the zero-shot language model constitutes strong baseline when read through the newline probability and outperforms the multilingual detector. Third, TurnTurk-GPT exceeds it only on the recording-disjoint split; on unseen speakers the difference is not significant, and the decrease of 0.028 between splits indicates that part of the information learned from six conversations is speaker-specific. Fourth, among the training configurations only S2R-SR is significant. Therefore no general benefit of synthetic pre-training can be claimed. Synthetic pre-training nevertheless improves calibration: the threshold reaching 70% recall is 0.00000 for and 0.016 for S2R. Although ranks decision points well, its turnshift probabilities remain below numerical precision, which prevents the selection of fixed threshold in deployed system. This improvement in calibration, rather than gain in AP, is the most evident contribution of the synthetic corpus. A. Main comparison B. Operating points Table II gives the results and Table III the paired comparisons. Under the speaker-disjoint split, S2R reaches AP 0.120. Fig. 2 shows the same comparison graphically with recording-level 95% bootstrap intervals; all bars refer to the recording-disjoint split except the one marked for unseen speakers, and the dashed line marks the random baseline of 0.037. Four observations can be made. First, TurnTurk-GPT AP summarises ranking over all thresholds, whereas deployed system operates at one. Table IV reports precision, false alarms per correct detection and the pre-pause false alarm rate when each systems threshold is set to reach 70% and 90% recall. Three observations follow from Table IV. First, at 70% recall the fine-tuned model produces approximately ten false S2R LM (newline) LM (.?!) FA/hit 16.0 17.5 15.2 21.8 51.7% .059 57.2% .054 50.9% .062 65.4% .044 PP 80.1% 82.0% 77.1% 88.0% alarms per correct detection, indicating that none of the textonly systems is suitable as stand-alone end-of-turn trigger. Second, at fixed recall the fine-tuned model and the zero-shot language model perform almost identically, and at 90% recall the zero-shot model is slightly ahead; the AP advantage of S2R on the recording-disjoint split therefore originates from its highest-confidence decisions at low recall. Third, both outperform the multilingual detector, which produces 16.0 false alarms per correct detection at 70% recall against 9.6 for S2R, and predicts turn end during speakers pause in 65.4% of cases against 51.7%. The difference in pre-pause false alarms between S2R and the zero-shot model in Table II is not present at matched recall; it reflects the different recall levels of the nested thresholds rather than difference between the models. C. When the speaker pauses voice agent typically queries its end-of-turn model when silence is detected. Restricting the evaluation to those moments, the 578 turn ends and the 633 turn-internal pauses, gives balanced binary task (Table V), on which random predictor scores AP 0.477. Both baselines remain close to chance level, indicating that textual information alone does not reliably distinguish completed turn from pause within turn. Prosodic and visual cues are natural candidates for resolving this case. D. Turkish-specific analyses Morphology: Table VI stems one word per turn to its first four characters in the test text, without retraining. Stemming the turn-final word reduces AP by 32% (R) and 44% (S2R); stemming random sentence-internal word changes it by 0.2% and 2.2%. Both drops are significant. The end-of-turn cue is TABLE PAUSE MOMENTS ONLY System LM (newline) LiveKit detector AP 0.590 0.530 AUC 0.630 0.537 TABLE VI TURKISH-SPECIFIC ANALYSES Variant Original Turn-final word stemmed Random internal word stemmed .116 .079 (32%) .116 (+0%) S2R .148 .083 (44%) .145 (2%) therefore located in the suffixes of the final, typically verbal, word. Backbone: The English GPT-2 tokeniser splits Turkish into 2.94 tokens per word against 1.17 for the Turkish one, distributing suffixes across several fragments; with this backbone, the AP of decreases from 0.116 to 0.042, close to the random baseline. Fine-tuning does not degrade the language modelling ability of the backbone: held-out perplexity falls from 282.1 to 272.8. E. Synthetic data Trained on synthetic dialogue alone, the model reaches AP 0.082, below the zero-shot language model, and it has the highest pre-pause false alarm rate of all systems (33.5%, Table II). Used for pre-training before real data, synthetic dialogue helps relative to mixing the corpora in one stage, whereas the difference relative to real data alone is not significant; its most evident benefit is calibration. VII. DISCUSSION A. Why the zero-shot model is strong baseline The newline reading of the untuned backbone outperforms the deployed multilingual detector and is within 0.02 AP of the fine-tuned model. plausible explanation is that in the backbones Turkish pre-training text, line breaks follow complete sentences more frequently than incomplete ones, so the probability of line break after word already estimates syntactic and morphological completeness. In Turkish that estimate is informative, because the clause-final verb and its suffixes mark completion; the morphology ablation in Section VI-D shows that the fine-tuned model relies on the same cue. The contribution of fine-tuning on six conversations consists mainly of familiarity with the speakers: the gain over the zero-shot model disappears on the speaker-disjoint split, while the gain over the multilingual detector persists. Where gain exists, it is limited to the highest-confidence decisions; at the recall levels relevant for deployment, the two models are equivalent (Table IV). This suggests that, at the present data scale, the limiting factor is speaker diversity rather than model capacity. It is therefore recommended that future studies on Turkish report the zero-shot newline baseline, since weaker reading of the same model would overstate any improvement approximately twofold. B. Implications for deployment VIII. CONCLUSION Three practical implications follow for Turkish voice agents based on speech recognition. First, statistical and practical significance do not coincide. The fine-tuned models +0.019 AP over the zero-shot model is significant on the recordingdisjoint split without yielding fewer false alarms at practical levels, whereas its advantage over the multilingual recall detector, approximately six fewer false alarms per correct detection at 70% recall, is of practical relevance. Second, multilingual detectors published operating threshold does not transfer: at its Turkish threshold the evaluated detector raised false alarm on 85.5% of pre-pause words, so system relying on this threshold would interrupt users at most hesitations. Thresholds should therefore be selected on in-domain data. Third, systems should be compared at matched recall. False alarm rates measured at each systems own optimal threshold can differ by factor of two between models that perform equivalently at the same recall, as Tables II and IV show. In absolute terms, approximately ten false alarms per correct detection at 70% recall indicate that text-only prediction of this kind is suited to complementing rather than replacing silencebased endpointing. C. Implications for synthetic dialogue Synthetic dialogue has been proposed as way to bootstrap turn-taking models for languages with little conversational data [10]. The present results qualify this proposal: used alone, synthetic dialogue produced the weakest trained model, and used for pre-training it yielded no significant gain over real data alone. likely cause is the generation process. Each synthetic turn is short, complete, well-formed sentence, with none of the mid-sentence pauses, self-repairs and resumptions that complicate turn-end detection in real conversation. Generators intended for this task should produce longer turns, sentences that span turns, and turns that pause and then continue. D. Scope of the evaluation The real corpus comprises six conversations with six distinct speakers. The speaker-disjoint split measures generalisation to speakers absent from training, and the difference between the two splits quantifies the share of the learned signal that is speaker-specific. The evaluation is performed offline on final transcripts in the normalised form described in Section IV-B. Evaluation on the partial hypotheses of streaming recogniser, together with its latency, is natural extension of this setting. Labels are derived from voice activity and mark the points at which the floor passes to the other speaker. Such points are closely related to, but not identical with, points at which response is appropriate: some turn ends invite no response, and some turn-internal pauses invite backchannel. The multilingual detector is evaluated at every word and at pause moments, independently of the production pipeline in which it is normally deployed, so that all systems are compared on the same decision points. This paper presented TurnTurk-GPT, text-based turntaking predictor for Turkish, and compared it with rule-based, zero-shot and deployed systems on real conversation under recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint splits, with paired significance tests throughout. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms widely used multilingual endof-turn detector on both splits, indicating that model trained on Turkish conversation is preferable to the multilingual alternative, including for unseen speakers. zero-shot Turkish language model, read through the probability of line break, constitutes strong baseline, which fine-tuning on six conversations surpasses only for familiar speakers; further gains therefore depend on speaker diversity rather than on the model. At the recall levels deployed system would use, TurnTurkGPT and the zero-shot model are equivalent, and both produce fewer false alarms than the multilingual detector. The analyses identify the source of the end-of-turn signal and its limits. The end-of-turn cue is carried by the suffixes of the turn-final word, consistent with the verb-final structure of Turkish, and an English tokeniser that fragments those suffixes reduces performance to near-chance level. Synthetic dialogue alone is weak training signal whose main benefit is calibration. When the speaker pauses, the text-only baselines are close to chance level, identifying case that text alone does not resolve. Three directions for future work follow. Collecting conversations from more speakers is the most direct way to improve generalisation, and the speaker-disjoint split measures it; since no open corpus of this kind exists for Turkish, such data would also benefit other work on Turkish spoken dialogue. Generating synthetic dialogue that reproduces the pauses and resumptions of real conversation may make the synthetic corpus useful beyond calibration. Finally, the corpuss separate audio channels and facial features make it possible to add prosodic and visual cues and to test whether they resolve the pause case. The model and the evaluation protocol are released so that these steps can be measured against the same baselines.
